fields.Front: Define relationship, relationship set and relationship type, using the Laura/CS3319 example.
fields.Back:
Relationship: a named grouping of entities - an association among two or more entities ('we're taking an instance of a prof entity and an instance of a course entity and grouping them together').
Relationship set: the ordered list, e.g. (Laura, CS3319).
Relationship type R among E1..En: a set of relationship instances ri, each associating n entities (e1..en) with ej from Ej - a mathematical relation. TEACHES is the relationship type.

fields.Front: Define the degree of a relationship and give the three kinds with examples.
fields.Back:
Degree = the number of entity types participating.
Unary/recursive (1): a relationship from an entity type to itself - EMPLOYEE SUPERVISES EMPLOYEE, with role names supervisor/supervisee.
Binary (2): the common case - Student TAKES Course (attribute Grade), Employee WORKS FOR Department.
Ternary (3): SUPPLIER supplies PART to PROJECT, relationship Supply with attribute Quantity.

fields.Front: Why can Homer's grade of 89 not be an attribute of STUDENT or of COURSE?
fields.Back: On STUDENT you cannot tell which course the 89 was for (CS2210 or CS3319); on COURSE you cannot tell which student earned it. Grade 'doesn't describe the student, it doesn't describe the course; it describes the COMBINATION', so it goes on the TAKES relationship.

fields.Front: Define cardinality ratio and give the case-study example of each of the three common ratios.
fields.Back:
Cardinality ratio = how many relationship instances an entity can participate in (a MAXIMUM).
1:1 - Employee MANAGES Department (an employee manages one department; a department has one manager).
N:1 - Employee WORKS FOR Department (an employee works for one department; a department has many employees).
M:N - Employee WORKS ON Project (an employee works on many projects; a project has many employees).

fields.Front: Describe the instructor's 'could' technique for finding a cardinality ratio, and the two wording rules.
fields.Back: Take one instance of the left entity and ask 'an X COULD relate to how many Y?'; write the answer beside Y. Then look at it backwards: 'a Y could relate to how many X?'; write that beside X. Rules: (1) use 'could', never 'must' - 'must' and 'every' belong to participation; (2) you are asking for the MAXIMUM ('a woman is currently married to how many men? It might be zero, but the most you can be is one').

fields.Front: Give the cardinality and reasoning for the three worked slide examples: artist/painting, person/pet, man fathers child.
fields.Back:
ARTIST (1) --- paints --- (M) PAINTING: normally a painting is painted by just one artist.
PERSON (1) --- owns --- (M) PET: in a vet's database you keep one person's name on file, so a pet has one owner; context decides.
Man BIOLOGICALLY FATHERS Child: 1:N - a man could father many children, a child has one father. 'Biologically' is deliberate: step-fathers or adoptive fathers would change the ratio.

fields.Front: How are 'currently married to' and 'was married to' between WOMAN and MAN modelled, and why M and N rather than M and M?
fields.Back:
Currently Married To: 1:1 with attribute Wedding Date ('in the great province of Ontario' you can currently be married to at most one).
Was Married To: M:N with Wedding Date and Marriage End Date, since over a lifetime each could have had many spouses.
She writes M and N so you do not think the two 'many' values must be equal (five ex-husbands does not mean five ex-wives); M and M is allowed. Woman-to-woman would be drawn as a UNARY relationship with the same ratios.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: a ternary Supply relationship records that supplier S sent 7 of part P for project J. Why can three binary relationships not replace it?
fields.Back: Quantity depends on all THREE together - 'it's not just for supplier, project or part, it's part of the relationship'. Three separate binary relationships could not record which part went to which project from which supplier, so the quantity would be meaningless.

fields.Front: In the WORKS FOR instance diagram (Laura, Roberto, e3, e4 on the left; Computer Science, Math, English on the right), how many entity types participate and what does that make the relationship?
fields.Back: Two - EMPLOYEE and DEPARTMENT - so WORKS FOR is a BINARY relationship. Laura has 'some sort of relationship r1' with Computer Science; Roberto has a different one, r2.

fields.Front: List the six case-study relationships with their cardinality ratios and attributes.
fields.Back:
MANAGES: EMPLOYEE 1 : DEPARTMENT 1, attribute StartDate
WORKS FOR: EMPLOYEE N : DEPARTMENT 1
CONTROLS: DEPARTMENT 1 : PROJECT N
WORKS ON: EMPLOYEE M : PROJECT N, attribute Hours
SUPERVISES: EMPLOYEE 1 : EMPLOYEE N (unary)
HAS / DEPENDENTS OF: EMPLOYEE 1 : DEPENDENT N (identifying)

fields.Front: What assumption lets a dependent belong to only one employee, and how does draw.io attach a relationship attribute?
fields.Back: That no married couples work at the company; otherwise a child could be the dependent of two employees. In draw.io: hover over the oval until the connection arrows appear, then drag a line to the diamond (Hours to 'works on', Start Date to 'is managed by').

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §3.4.4): when may an attribute of a binary relationship type be migrated onto a participating entity type?
fields.Back:
1:1 - to EITHER side, because each entity participates in at most one instance, so the value is determined by either end. Start_date on MANAGES could sit on EMPLOYEE or on DEPARTMENT.
1:N - only to the entity type on the N SIDE, because each N-side entity is in at most one instance while a 1-side entity is in many, each with a different value. A Start_date on WORKS_FOR can go on EMPLOYEE, never on DEPARTMENT.
M:N - NEVER: the value is determined by the COMBINATION of participating entities, not by either entity alone, so it must stay a relationship attribute. Hours on WORKS_ON is the example.
For 1:1 and 1:N the placement is 'determined subjectively by the schema designer'; conceptually the attribute still belongs to the relationship. This is also why mapping steps 3 and 4 only add columns while step 5 must create a new table.

fields.Text: In Chen notation a relationship type is a {{c1::diamond}} with lines to each participating entity; an attribute on the relationship is an {{c1::oval joined to the diamond}}; the cardinality letters {{c1::1, M or N}} go on the lines.

An attribute belongs on a relationship when its value depends on the {{c1::pair (or triple)}}, not on one entity alone: {{c1::Grade}} depends on (student, course), {{c1::Hours}} on (employee, project) and Quantity on (supplier, part, project).
For Employee WORKS FOR Department, the letter {{c1::N}} is written beside EMPLOYEE and {{c1::1}} beside DEPARTMENT; putting the letter on the wrong side is a classic {{c1::exam trap}}.

The case-study relationship that is 'not one of the obvious ones' is the unary {{c1::SUPERVISES}}: an employee supervises {{c1::many}} employees and is supervised by {{c1::one}} boss. StartDate sits on MANAGES and Hours on WORKS ON.

The degree of a relationship is the number of {{c1::entity types}} in it: {{c1::unary/recursive}} (EMPLOYEE SUPERVISES EMPLOYEE, with role names supervisor and supervisee), {{c1::binary}} (the common case) and ternary (Supplier supplies Part to Project, attribute Quantity).

Textbook (Elmasri §3.4.1): NOTATION - what the instructor calls a relationship set (Laura first, CS3319 second) is the textbook's {{c1::relationship instance}}; the textbook's relationship SET is {{c1::the set of all such instances}}, and mathematically it is a subset of the {{c1::Cartesian product}} of the participating entity sets.

Textbook (Elmasri §3.4.2): NOTATION - the instructor's {{c1::unary}} relationship is the textbook's {{c1::recursive (self-referencing)}} relationship, and role names are technically necessary only when {{c1::the same entity type participates more than once}}, since otherwise the entity type's own name serves as the role name.
